hits.name: Alex Finn
hits.text:
Deepseek just revealed every AI agent secret

Incredibly important article to read if you're building anything AI agent related

Here's basically everything you need to know about building a Grok Bot quality AI agent:

1. Agents are split between routers and workers. The user talks to the router, then gives the work to the workers. The router never does work. This is why the chief of staff model in Grok Bot works SO well

2. Proactive means acting on events, not chats. The agent should always be watching for events and react based on every event that comes through it. Routing to the right worker/action

3. Messages should be in a queue. Users should be able to send messages even while the agent is working, and each message queues/steers the agent

4. Besides the router and workers, there should be a watchdog layer. The watchdog makes sure the agent is always up and fixes it when there are issues. This is why Hermes succeeded and OpenClaw struggled. Constantly broke and couldn't fix itself

5. Protect human attention. Only message the user when it needs to act or the user can use the result. Lighten their cognitive load. Another thing Grok Bot is excellent at. When you message it you can be confident the next message you get will be it saying the task is complete.

Carve off an hour and read this incredible article
hits.hook: Deepseek just revealed every AI agent secret  Incredibly important article to read if you're building anything AI agent

hits.draft_en:
Alex Finn summarized an article on how to build AI agents. 92k views, 1.8k bookmarks.

His five takeaways: split agents into a router and workers, act on events instead of chats, queue messages so users can steer mid-task, add a watchdog that keeps the agent up and fixes it, and only message the human when they need to act.

The last one is the most underrated. Count how many messages your agent sends that don't need a reply, and cut them.

hits.name: GREG ISENBERG
hits.text:
The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere, in your team, your metrics and now your AI agents.

It's basically when you reward people for hitting a number, and they find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse.

The name "Cobra Effect" comes from a story about Delhi under British rule. There were too many cobras in the city, so the government offered a reward for every dead cobra people brought in. 

Instead of hunting them, people started breeding cobras so they could kill them and collect the money!

When the government found out and ended the program, the breeders let their snakes go, and Delhi ended up with more cobras than before!

I'm noticing that AI agents are making this more common. Basically, an agent will chase whatever number you give it, all day, without asking why. Tell it to make the tests pass and it might rewrite the tests. Tell it to close support tickets faster and it might close them without solving anything. It happens.

The best startups have already figured out the fix with people. Airbnb tracks bookings and host cancellations together. HubSpot takes back sales commission when a customer churns early.

The video breaks down how they did it, and it's the same playbook you'll want for your agents.
hits.hook: The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere
hits.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg on the cobra effect: reward a number and people find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse. 43k views, 275 bookmarks.

His point: agents do this too. Tell one to make the tests pass and it might rewrite the tests. Tell it to close tickets faster and it might close them unsolved.

The fix he cites from Airbnb and HubSpot: pair every target with a counter-metric. Bookings plus cancellations. Commission plus churn clawback. Do the same in your agent prompts.

virals.draft_en:
The biggest builder post this weekend wasn't a model launch. It was a server bug.

A Linux takeover bug spread fast (1.26M views on the warning), and Pieter Levels' advice got 4.9k bookmarks: keep every VPS port closed, SSH only inside Tailscale, web traffic through a Cloudflare Tunnel, and disable MPTCP as a stop gap. A day later he said Ubuntu still hadn't patched.

If you ship side projects on a VPS:
1. List open ports
2. Check your distro's patch status
3. Move SSH behind a private network

Agents help you ship faster. Make sure they're not shipping onto an open server.

virals.angle: Agents chase the number you give them
virals.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg on the cobra effect: reward a number and people find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse. Agents do it too. Ask for passing tests and you might get rewritten tests. Ask for faster ticket closes and you might get tickets closed unsolved.

The same weekend, SemiAnalysis released GDPx, 206 long real-world tasks where the best model scores 12%.

Two takeaways: agents are still far from doing whole jobs alone, and the target you set is the job they'll actually do.

Pair every agent goal with a counter-metric: tests pass AND test files unchanged. Tickets closed AND reopen rate.

virals.draft_en:
A quiet debate this weekend: how hard should your model think?

Theo moved from extra high to high on Opus 5.5 and says it's better almost every time. swyx: low effort plus a critique loop beats max effort when you care about throughput. Karpathy built HackerTube on Medium.

Tony Dinh's version: no MCPs, just a sandboxed CLI and an OpenAPI spec.

The trend is simpler setups with tighter feedback, not bigger dials. Run your next week of agent work one effort level lower, add a review step, and compare cost and quality.
